As a person that was born and raised in the Czech Republic after the Velvet Revolution and also as a person who was effectively bombarded with stories of all the vile and awful things our communist secret police (and the regular police too, for that matter) were capable of doing to the citizens of the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic  (ČSSR) during the time of its existence, I think it was not surprising to me that my reaction to this video was not "Oh, that's horrible" but more "I could definitely see this happening." And when it was revealed that there were two people in conversation, both of whom were snitching on each other to the secret police, I effectively burst out laughing, it was like "There it is, those are the secret police tactics I heard so much about, and how effective it is when citizens take part to uphold socialism against its will to destroy itself."

I recall my dad, who became a plumber by trade after the regime fell, telling me a story about how one of their neighbours was definitely a snitch -- if not to the police then at least to the City council (or Národní výbor), more of an open secret than a rumor now that I think about it. Apparently, this neighbour once called my dad, this is about 20 years after the revolution, mind you, to repair his boiler or something like that.  I don't know if my dad needed every job he could get or if he did not care that much or if he was more kind to these sort of things back then or what, but he did go to his house to do the job.  Apparently, the atmosphere was rather heavy from the very start -- the neighbour was quite old at this point, so of course he stayed home as my dad was working and was pretty much standing behind his back the entire time. Suddenly, he started saying some things regarding the things he did during the communist regime, how apologetic he was for his actions as a snitch or something. My dad said something to the effect of "Do not say a word more. I'm here to do a job, and that's it. Nothing more, nothing less." I think he also warned him that if he did not shut up, he could not guarantee that the neighbour’s nose would be in one piece after he leaves. So the neighbour did shut up at the end and got his plumbing fixed, paid the money and that was that...

This kind of historical uneasiness is to this day even more prevalent than one might think. As a matter of fact, in the last presidential election in Czechia (which was last year, mind you!), the personal relationship to the communist party of both final two presidential candidates was scrutinized by the media and public alike. While one was definitely in training to become a member of the communist army as some kind of special forces operative, the other was found as a snitch (or collaborator, as we say) in the secret police files, allegedly. I have to say allegedly, because I do not want to get sued. The former candidate won, by the way, as he was appointed Chair of the NATO Military Committee after communism was expelled from our country, regaining the nation’s trust in the process. While the other guy became a rich entrepreneur, utilizing the chaos and unlawful practices in the free-for-all nature of the economy in the turbulent nineties and effectively holds most of the country’s agricultural sector under his belt. Again, allegedly.  But he did get quite a lot of votes regardless and is currently the leader of the most popular (and populist) political party in Czechia, according to the polls at least.

The secret police of ČSSR was probably not as organized and as efficient as the Stasi, the Germans were always better at that sort of thing after all, but it did apparently do some similar operations described in this video. I recall watching a documentary on precisely this sort of thing. They interviewed one person who was subject to a similar fate to Mr. Templin, though not as brutal, he was not some human rights activist. No, instead, his ‘crime’ was that before the Soviet invasion to the ČSSR in 1968, he utilized the more open borders, travelled abroad and did not come back after the tanks rolled into Prague. Later, he got word that one of his family members was ill, wanted to see them and somehow was allowed back. Not for free, of course, he had to pay the price of being monitored from pretty much the moment his plane touched down back home. In the documentary, he describes reading ‘his file’ the police had on him after the revolution, or whatever was left of it and not destroyed, anyway. Pictures of him crossing the street, taken covertly by a camera hidden in a woman’s purse. How many times they visited his home. Phone conversation logs. That time he said hello to a random man when getting out of the car and how this man who he did not even know was then automatically subject to surveillance of his own, seeing if that was some hidden communication code or something. There was nothing, of course. He also recalled how initially, the visits to his home were covert, he was just informed of them by the person living in the next-door apartment. Later, they made their visits more and more obvious, and more frequent. Furniture thrown about, drawers opened and scattered across the room. The next-door neighbour talked about just how many people went into that apartment every time. You’d think that man would recount these memories like war stories, eyes full of horror and broken spirit. But surprisingly even to me, he was more jolly about it than anything else. One of his final lines in the documentary explained this sentiment: “Gee, if only they took all that money and resources they put into surveillance of people like me and redirected them into, I don’t know, making this country better for the people, we could have actually been living quite well under this socialism.” You can’t break a man with that sort of attitude.

Of course, these things manifested themselves in art as well. I especially recommend you watch “The Ear”, ‘Ucho’ in Czech, filmed in 1969, banned to screen in theatres by the communists and officially released twenty years later, pretty much right after the revolution, directed by Karel Kachyňa. I think you can find it with English subtitles somewhere. It tells the tale of a relatively low-level government official and his wife who find their home wiretapped and bugged. It takes place largely in one house and consists of mostly two characters, portrayed masterfully by brilliant actors. In Czech, they apparently called these hidden microphones ‘ears’, hence the name of the movie. I believe it is an excellent psychological thriller which showcases exactly how this type of surveillance can mentally break you.

I thank the creators of this video for covering this topic, while not talked about on the English part of the internet, it is still important to this day. The guys that did these things are still out there, if they haven’t died already. Similarly to the leader of the Stasi, a lot of them were never prosecuted -- for their communist crimes, at least. There is a reason that many crimes committed during the regime do not have a statute of limitations here in Czechia. And most importantly, the communist party, or more precisely their rebranded party and associated parties, was in the parliament for some election cycles even after the revolution and now that they are not, they are trying to crawl back there. Once again, immense thanks.
